transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith... I only came in because, well, they made me. My family, I mean. And my friends. So-called friends, really. They keep... they keep bringing out all these bank papers, right? Sticking them right in my face, pointing at the numbers and saying they prove nothing was taken. Like I'm some kind of idiot who can
Aside from feeling that things have been taken from you, have you ever heard voices or sounds that other people couldn't hear, or seen things that others didn't see?

Voices? No. No, I don't... why would you even ask me something like that? I'm not crazy. I mean, I know that's what they want you to think, my family and everyone, but my hearing is perfectly fine. I don't hear people whispering in my head or, I don't know, ghosts or whatever it is people hear. The only voices I hear are the ones right in the room with me, and half the time they're lying to my face anyway. 

And I definitely don't see things that aren't there either. My eyes are good. I never even needed glasses, not even when I was a kid back in school, I always had perfect vision. So I see exactly what's right in front of me, clear as day. I don't see imaginary things, I see the real things, like how the numbers on those papers they keep shoving at me don't add up, no matter how fast they try to snatch them away and change the subject. 

They probably told you to ask me that, didn't they? About the voices. They probably called ahead and said, oh, make sure you ask if she's hearing things, just to make me sound like I'm losing my mind so they can just keep what's mine and get away with it. But no, no voices, no visions, nothing like that. My mind is completely sharp. I only see and hear what's actually happening.
Have you had any recent head injury, illness, new medications, or drug or alcohol use around the time these beliefs about money being taken started?

Beliefs? First of all, they aren't beliefs, Dr. Smith. It is just what's actually happening. But no. No to all of that. I haven't hit my head. I haven't been sick, not even a cold, I take very good care of myself. I always make sure I'm eating right and taking care of my health even when I
How long have you believed that your family and friends have been taking your money?

There you go again with that word, believed. It's not a belief, Dr. Smith, it's a fact. And I know exactly when it started, too. It wasn't just some random day where I woke up and decided to make this all up. No, this has been going on for about a year and two months. Exactly since my income dropped. 

I remember it so clearly because, well, when you don't have a lot of money coming in, you have to watch every single penny, right? You have to. You count what you have, you know exactly what's in your pocket, you know what's supposed to be in the account. So, about fourteen months ago, my income goes down, and suddenly... things are just missing. And they probably thought I wouldn't notice. They probably all sat around and thought, oh, she's just confused because she doesn't have as much coming in now, she'll just think she spent it, she won't know the difference. 

But I'm not stupid. I might not have finished high school, but I know how to count my own money. I know what I had before that drop, and I know exactly what's been taken since. Right when I was most vulnerable, right when my money situation changed a year and two months ago, that's when they swooped in. And it's been fourteen months of this. Fourteen months of them pretending to be my friends, pretending to care about me, asking how I'm doing, while they just bleed me dry and then shove those fake bank papers in my face to cover their tracks. They think they're so smart, doing it right when my income changed, but I saw exactly what they did.
Aside from the money situation, do you feel that people are trying to harm you, control you, or plot against you in any other ways?

Harm me? Like... physically hurt me? No. No, why would they do that? I mean, it's not like I think someone's hiding in the bushes outside my place or, you know, trying to poison my food or something crazy like that. I watch TV, I know what people do when they want to actually hurt someone, and it's not that.
Aside from this issue with your family and friends about money, how have you been managing with your daily routine, work, and relationships otherwise?

Well, my routine is... it's fine. It's exactly what it needs to be. I mean, other than the constant arguments about the money, which, honestly, take up so much of my time because I have to keep checking everything they touch, but other than that? I'm completely fine. I still handle my own meals every single day. I go to the grocery store, I pick out exactly what I need, I cook for myself. I don't need anyone doing that for me. And I get myself to the county clinic, I make sure I'm there early, actually, because if you're late they just push you to the back of the line and I don't have time for that. I get to all my assistance appointments on time, too. I sit in those waiting rooms with my paperwork in a folder, all organized, because you have to be organized when you're dealing with the county, you know? 

And my place is clean. I keep my things in order the exact same way I always have, since before any of this started. Everything has a place. My clothes are folded, my dishes are washed. I'm not falling apart, Dr. Smith. People might think, oh, she's losing her money, she must be a mess, she must be letting everything go. But I'm not. I'm managing perfectly well. It's just the relationships that are... well, you can imagine how hard it is to sit across from someone, having a cup of coffee, when you know for a fact they took twenty dollars from your kitchen counter the week before. It changes how you talk to them. It changes everything. But my daily life? My routine? No, I take care of myself just fine. Better than fine, really, considering what I have to deal with.
Over this past year, have you noticed any big changes in your mood—like feeling unusually sad, hopeless, or on the other hand, unusually energetic or elated—that lasted for weeks at a time?

Unusually sad? I mean... no. Not sad. Sad is, you know, when you watch a depressing movie on TV or somebody's dog gets run over. What I am is aggravated. But not hopeless, no. Because, think about it, Dr. Smith, if I was hopeless, I'd just let them take everything, wouldn't I? I'd just roll over in bed and say, 'Here, take my last dollar, take the change right out of my coat pocket, I don't care.' But I do care. I don't just let it happen. I check my things. I count my cash. So I'm definitely not hopeless. 

And elated? Like, really happy and bouncing off the walls? Why on earth would I be happy? My own family is stealing from me! You'd have to be completely out of your mind to be elated about a situation like that. I mean, sure, I have the energy to get up and go to the county clinic and get my groceries and keep my house clean, like I just told you, but I'm not... I'm not unusually energetic or running around for weeks at a time. I'm just alert. I'm awake. You have to be alert when people are trying to pull a fast one on you every chance they get. 

Sometimes I get mad, sure. I get really, really mad when I see a bank paper that doesn't match up with what I know I had, or when my sister looks me right in the eye and asks if I need a loan. A loan! From my own money that she probably took! But that's just normal mad. That's exactly how anyone would feel if they were in my shoes. It's not some... mood thing that just happens for weeks for no reason. If you want to know my mood, my mood is just tired. I'm tired of the lies and the pretending. But I don't sit around crying all day, if that's what you're asking. I don't have the time to sit around feeling sorry for myself. I have to keep track of my life. So no, I haven't noticed anything like that. My mood is just normal for what I'm being put through.
